fact: Colorado 811 says private lines, such as sprinkler systems, gas lines to backyard grills, invisible fences, septic systems, buried water tanks and service lines, are not part of an 811 locate and must be located at the owner's expense by a private locating company.
quote: Private Utilities: Often owned and operated by property owners, such as homeowners. These private utilities serve individual properties and include systems like sprinkler systems, gas lines to backyard grills, invisible fences, septic systems, buried water tanks and service lines. Private utilities are not registered with Colorado 811, are not part of an 811 locate request, and must be located at the owner's expense by a private locating company. … Don’t forget that 811 does not mark private lines such as gas grill lines, septic systems, invisible fences, sprinklers, or buried tanks. For private utilities, contact a private locating firm prior to excavation.
source_label: Colorado 811, Private Underground Utility Information
notes: Read with curl 2026-09-25. The same page carries a directory of private locating companies with a filter for every Colorado county, Larimer and Weld included.

fact: Colorado 811 tells homeowners that utilities mark only the lines they own, that marking private lines such as sprinkler lines and gas lines is the property owner's responsibility, and that landscaping needs a locate: don't rely only on the landscaper, and if in doubt contact 811 yourself.
quote: Landscaping (Don’t just rely on your landscaper to do it, if in doubt, contact 811 yourself). … There may be private utilities within your dig area such as sprinkler lines, gas lines, or a BBQ, that require you to higher a private locating company in addition to calling 811. Private Utilities are lines on your property not owned by a public utility company. It is your responsibility to have private utilities marked before digging. Colorado 811 does not mark private utility lines. … Public utility companies will mark only the lines that they own.
source_label: Colorado 811, Residential Property: Planning to Dig on Your Property?
notes: "higher" (for hire) is the page's own typo, kept verbatim. The same page says both "at least 48 hours (excluding weekends, the day of the notification, and legal holidays)" and "Wait at least 3 full business days"; copy uses the statute's two business days for the legal minimum and the three-business-day advice from 811 and the PUC.

fact: Colorado 811 says any digging, however shallow, needs a locate first, including digging by hand, grading and scraping, and that digging can start once every utility in the area has posted an all-clear and the marks are visible.
quote: No matter how shallow or how deep you are digging, you must contact 811 first for any excavation including digging by hand, digging with machinery, grading, scraping, trenching, tunnelling, plowing—and more. … You can start digging once all markings or flags are clearly visible on the ground of your excavation areas and you receive a status update from all utilities located in your excavation area indicating an all clear.
source_label: Colorado 811, Residential Property: Planning to Dig on Your Property? (FAQ)

fact: Colorado 811 says private locate services average $100 to $350, depending on the company and the property's type and size, while the 811 locate of public lines is free.
quote: Public utility companies will mark only the lines that they own. To find out If you have private utilities within your dig area, you’ll need to contact a private locate company to mark the location of these utilities. Fees for private locate services in average range from $100 to $350, depending on the company you use and the property type and size located. … It's free! There is no cost to have public underground utility lines located on your property.
source_label: Colorado 811, Residential Property: Your Second Call: Private Utility Locating Companies/Services
notes: A range 811 publishes for private locators, not a NoCo price.

fact: Colorado 811 says utility locators mark lines within 3 business days, that the area must be open to locate crews during that time with no locked gates and no animals, that private lines come after the public ticket is confirmed, and that within 18 inches of a mark you dig only by hand, if at all.
quote: If so, contact a private locate company after you receive confirmation of your public locate utility ticket from Colorado 811. … Utility company locators will mark your lines within 3 business days. … During the 3-day period after you get your email confirmation, be sure the area to be marked is completely accessible to locate crews. No locked gates No animals … The area within 18 inches of utility marks in every direction is called the tolerance zone. In this zone, dig only by hand, if at all.
source_label: Colorado 811, What to Know Before You Dig

fact: If a utility line is hit, Colorado 811 says to get to safety, call 911 in an emergency, and report the damage to Colorado 811 right away.
quote: Get to safety and call 911 in an emergency. Report a utility line damage to Colorado 811 right away by calling 811
source_label: Colorado 811, Residential Property: I hit a utility line! What do I do now?

fact: Colorado's Public Utilities Commission says 811 does not locate private lines such as sprinkler lines or electric fences, advises contacting 811 at least three business days ahead, and lists the mark colors: red electric, yellow gas, blue drinking water, orange communication lines, purple reclaimed water, irrigation and slurry lines, green sewers and drains, white proposed excavation, pink temporary survey marks.
quote: Call 811 or visit Colorado811.org a minimum of three business days before starting any excavation project. Colorado 811 will notify the public utilities in your dig area, who will send a locator to mark the location of the public underground utility lines - Colorado 811 does not locate private utility lines such as sprinkler system lines or electric fences. The 811 service is completely free. Markings will be placed via paint or flags. The following colors indicate what type of public utility is below: Red = Electric Yellow = Gas Blue = Potable Water Orange = Communication lines such as cable TV or Internet Purple = Reclaimed Water, Irrigation and Slurry Lines Green = Sewers and Drain lines White = Proposed excavation Pink = Temporary Survey Markings
source_label: Colorado Public Utilities Commission, press release, March 31, 2026: Governor Jared Polis Declares April 2026 'Dig Safely Month'
notes: The colors follow the American Public Works Association uniform color code (apwa.org blocks automated fetch; the statute requires that code).

fact: Colorado law says a person may not begin excavation without first notifying the notification association (Colorado 811), at least two business days ahead, not counting the day of notice.
quote: a person shall not make or begin excavation without first notifying the notification association. Notice may be given by electronic methods approved by the notification association or by telephone. (b) Notice of the commencement, extent, and duration of the excavation work shall be given at least two business days prior thereto not including the day of actual notice.
source_label: C.R.S. 9-1.5-103(3)(a)(II) and (3)(b), Colorado Revised Statutes 2022 printout posted by the Division of Oil and Public Safety
notes: Read in the state PDF (uncertified 2022 printout). The same wording appears in the 2024 CRS text as reproduced by colorado.public.law (read 2026-09-25); leg.colorado.gov's own CRS PDFs return 403 to automated fetch. The civil penalties for not notifying (9-1.5-104.5) exclude a homeowner working on their own property, so the practical duty falls on the person digging.

fact: Colorado law defines excavation to include grading and scraping, and excludes only routine maintenance on existing planted landscapes, meaning yearly work that does not dig more than four inches by machine and is not meant to permanently lessen the ground cover or lower the ground.
quote: "Excavation" means any operation in which earth is moved or removed by means of any tools, equipment, or explosives and includes augering, backfilling, boring, ditching, drilling, grading, plowing-in, pulling-in, ripping, scraping, trenching, hydro excavating, postholing, and tunneling. "Excavation" does not include: (a) Routine maintenance on existing planted landscapes; … (6.5) "Routine maintenance" means a regular activity that happens at least once per year on an existing planted landscape if earth is not disturbed at a depth of more than twelve inches by nonmechanical means or four inches by mechanical means and if the activities are not intended to permanently lessen the ground cover or lower the existing ground contours.
source_label: C.R.S. 9-1.5-102(3) and (6.5), Colorado Revised Statutes 2022 printout posted by the Division of Oil and Public Safety
notes: That replacing a lawn with turf falls outside routine maintenance is our reading (it permanently removes the ground cover and lowers the grade), labelled not legal advice in copy.

fact: Colorado law treats locate marks as valid only while they are clearly visible and for no more than 30 calendar days; if the excavation isn't finished in that time, the excavator must notify 811 again before the period ends.
quote: (b) The marking of underground facilities shall be considered valid so long as the markings are clearly visible, but not for more than thirty calendar days following the due date of the locate request initiated pursuant to subsection (3) of this section. If an excavation has not been completed within the thirty-day period, the excavator shall notify the notification association at least two business days, not including the day of actual notice, before the end of the thirty-day period.
source_label: C.R.S. 9-1.5-103(4)(b), Colorado Revised Statutes 2022 printout posted by the Division of Oil and Public Safety
notes: Same wording in the 2024 CRS text reproduced by colorado.public.law (read 2026-09-25).

fact: Little Thompson Water District says its locate runs from the water main to the meter pit, and the customer is responsible for locating the service line between the meter pit and the house and anything connected to it.
quote: Please call three days before you dig to give the locate team time to come out and mark your utilities. Locates for your water utility are from the main water line to the meter pit. You are responsible for locating the service line between your home and the meter pit and any connections to that line.
source_label: Little Thompson Water District, Call Before You Dig in Colorado | Call 811
notes: LTWD serves Mead, Barefoot Lakes in Firestone and Berthoud-area customers (ltwd-service-area-mead-barefoot-lakes, ltwd-watch-2026); Berthoud town-water customers should ask the Town where its locate stops.

fact: Colorado's Energy and Carbon Management Commission says its public flowline map shows approximate locations only, does not include every flowline in the ground, and that Colorado 811 must be used to locate any flowline precisely.
quote: Generally, they do not represent an on-the-ground survey and represent only the approximate relative location of flowlines. … Flowline spatial information is not designed nor intended to replace the Colorado 811 program for locating underground utility infrastructures. … Flowlines shown on the ECMC interactive map only include lines that have been vetted and approved by staff, and do not represent all of the flowlines that are currently in the ground. … For precise locating of any flowlines, Colorado 811 must be used.
source_label: Colorado Energy & Carbon Management Commission, Flowlines - GIS Data
notes: The brief asked whether oil and gas flowlines are in 811 locates before the page says anything: ECMC says 811 is the way to locate them. We did not confirm how abandoned lines are marked, so copy says nothing about them.

fact: Under Johnstown's 2026 Level 3 schedule (2 watering days a week, none from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., April 20 to October 15), the Town says sprinkler servicing that can't fit the assigned days should be raised with its conservation staff ahead of time.
quote: Under Level 3, the Level 2 standards restrictions and exemptions still apply, with the addition that the property's designated watering day are reduced to 2 times a week. These restrictions are in place from April 20 to October 15, 2026. Watering between the hours of 10 a.m. - 6 p.m., is NOT permitted at any time. … It is understood that system servicing or reactivation may prevent full alignment with the assigned watering schedule. If you anticipate any issues meeting your designated watering days, please contact conserve@johnstownco.gov to discuss your situation.
source_label: Town of Johnstown, Water FAQs: Water Conservation Schedule (What if I need to service my irrigation system?)

fact: Tarkett's synthetic grass installation manual says irrigation and electrical lines may lie just under the surface, tells installers to locate all irrigation lines and heads, cap or remove unwanted irrigation and test for leaks before starting, notes that rain-soaked soil may need a few days to dry, and has the area lightly wetted before the base is compacted.
quote: Rain-soaked soil may need a few days to dry before work begins. … Irrigation and electrical lines may be located just under the surface of the project area. Locate all irrigation lines, including sprinkler heads. Cap off or remove all unwanted irrigation. Test for leaks and verify that everything works correctly before you start. Do the same with any existing electrical features. … Lightly wet the project area and compact the base material with a roller compactor or plate compactor.
source_label: Tarkett Home, On the Green synthetic grass Installation Manual (PDF)

fact: Tarkett's installation manual says to turn the irrigation on after the turf is down to check that heads are capped and pipes weren't punctured, check the lighting, and finish all repairs before infill goes on.
quote: Turn on irrigation to check that all sprinklers heads are capped and pipes have not been punctured. Check all electrical lighting. All repair work must be completed prior to adding infill to the artificial grass.
source_label: Tarkett Home, On the Green synthetic grass Installation Manual (PDF), installation step I

fact: PetSafe's in-ground fence manual says to bury the boundary wire in a trench 1 to 3 inches deep so it isn't damaged and the system isn't disabled, and lists digging around landscaping as a common cause of wire breaks.
quote: Burying the Boundary Wire is recommended to protect it and prevent disabling the system. 1. Cut a trench 1-3 inches deep along your planned boundary. … Wire breaks in the Boundary Wire are commonly found: 1. In aerated lawns … 3. Around landscaping and flower beds due to digging or working up the soil
source_label: PetSafe Basic In-Ground Fence Operating and Training Guide (PIG00-14582)

fact: Ryan's Jr Sod Cutter spec sheet gives a cutting thickness adjustable up to 2.5 inches and a machine width of 25 inches.
quote: Cutting Thickness Adjustable up to 2.5 in. (64 mm) … Width 25 in. (635 mm)
source_label: Ryan Jr. Sod Cutter spec sheet (manufacturer PDF, dealer-hosted copy)
notes: The manufacturer's own spec sheet, read from a dealer's copy because ryanturf.com returned 404 and shop.ryanturf.com redirects behind a 403. Ryan's operator manual (precisionusa.com copy) also warns to check for underground utilities before cutting sod.

fact: VOLT Lighting says low-voltage landscape lighting cable is typically buried at least 6 inches deep, with the exact depth set by the local electrical code.
quote: Low voltage cable is typically buried at least 6 inches deep, though exact requirements depend on your local electrical code.
source_label: VOLT Lighting, How to Install Landscape Lighting

fact: Toro says its narrow-track Dingo TX 1000 compact utility loader is under 35 inches wide, which lets it through a standard 36-inch gate, and weighs 2,826 pounds.
quote: With a width of under 35 inches, the Dingo TX 1000 TURBO narrow track effortlessly navigates through standard 36-inch gates … Weight 2,826 lbs / 1,282 kg
source_label: Toro, Dingo TX 1000 TURBO Track Loader, Narrow (model 22587)
notes: One common machine of this class, used only to show why gate width matters; not a statement of what any installer uses.

fact: CSU Extension says a tree's protected root zone starts with the area under its dripline, roots reach beyond it, compacted or clay soils may need more room, and inside that zone there should be no grading, trenching, parking or stockpiling of materials.
quote: This zone is defined as the area beneath the dripline of the tree, although roots will extend beyond that area. … Inside the PRZ there can be NO grading, trenching, parking, stock piling of building materials or dumping of waste products. … Additional space may be needed on compacted or clayey soils.
source_label: CSU Extension, Tree Preservation During Construction (reviewed August 2023)
notes: Written for construction sites; the page applies it only to where machines drive and material is piled on install day. Turf around trees is its own guide (artificial-turf-around-trees).
